title: Sephiria Co-op Guide — 4-Player Runs, Trading & Revives (1.0)
description: Sephiria co-op guide: how four-player runs change enemy pressure, what to trade, how revives work, and which builds carry a party.
meta: Covers sephiria co-op / coop / four-player run searches; lobby setup lives on the multiplayer page. Includes role splits, a per-floor routine and troubleshooting.
body:
Co-op in Sephiria is online Steam co-op for up to four players, and it changes how a run plays: enemy pressure scales with the party, and the group can trade items and revive each other. For lobby setup, start with the multiplayer setup page — this page is about actually playing together.

What changes in co-op

SystemSingle playerIn co-op
Party sizeOneUp to four players, joined through Steam invites
EnemiesBaseline density and healthReported to scale with the number of players
ItemsYours onlyYou can trade items with the party
DeathRun overA teammate can revive you mid-run
Loot pressureEverything is yoursArtifact and Tablet competition is real — agree grid priorities before the run

Before floor one: the five-minute setup

  1. Confirm the party. Four is the cap, and every player needs the prologue and tutorial done first — the multiplayer page covers the lobby itself.
  2. Agree the grid split. Tablets and Artifacts are the contested pickups, so name who spends Tablets on what before anyone opens a shop.
  3. Name a revive order. Two players converging on the same body is one wasted defender; pick who goes first and who covers.
  4. Set the difficulty. Hard Mode is a per-run choice and scaling punishes a carried player, so match it to the weakest member rather than the strongest.
  5. Count active items, not stored ones. Side Bag storage disables effects, Tablets included, so anything parked there is dead weight for the whole party.

Splitting roles with documented systems

The six weapon branches already carry different jobs, and a party only needs each job once. The branch identities come from the weapons page and the routes from builds; the party column is our reading, not a game rule.

RoleBuilt fromJob in the partyWhat it costs
Front lineSword and Shield, or GreatswordHolds the line and anchors the reviveShort reach on Sword and Shield; long commitment per swing on Greatsword
ControlDagger frost routes such as Dormant Frost into DrifaLocks normal enemies so the damage player can workBoth enhancement slots go to the frost line, so the run is committed early
RangedCrossbowSafe damage while melee holds positionReload discipline
Body countCompanion / summonerSummons draw enemy attention away from the playersNeeds the Companion pieces actually active; stored ones do nothing
Revive dutyWhoever is least committed to a damage windowOne reviver per down while the rest protect the attemptThat player gives up damage uptime on that floor

Branch identities and trade-offs are the weapons page’s; the frost route is community-reported at 1.0.x. Which player takes which row is a party decision, not a documented rule.

Co-op builds that pull their weight

  • Companion / summoner — summons soak aggro, which is worth more in a party than solo. See the companion build.
  • Freeze control (Dagger route) — locking down normal enemies lets the damage player work. See builds.
  • Tank sword and shield — block and reflect builds are the natural revive-buddy role.
  • Ranged crossbow — safe damage while melee players hold the line.

Practical co-op habits

  • Agree the grid split before floor one. Tablets and Artifacts are shared loot, so decide who spends Tablets on what.
  • Trade duplicates instead of vendoring them. Item trading is built in, so a drop you cannot use may complete a teammate's route.
  • Keep one player on revive duty. Revives are the single biggest co-op advantage — a party that ignores them plays harder than solo.
  • Match difficulty to the weakest member. Enemy scaling makes a carried player a liability, and Hard Mode is a per-run choice.
  • Expect host-authoritative progress. The session belongs to the host, so a host disconnect is the usual cause of a broken lobby.

A routine for each floor

  1. Before the door: restate the grid split if a shop or Anvil is coming up, because a Tablet decision gets harder once the offer is on screen.
  2. During the fight: keep the front line or control player between the enemy and the ranged player, and let summons take the first contact in a crowded room.
  3. On a down: call the name and the room, then send one player. Crowding the prompt costs the party a defender.
  4. After a boss: re-check the board. Adjacency and edge constraints force reshuffles, so last floor’s Tablet placement may not survive the fight.
  5. When a duplicate drops: offer it to the player whose core it completes rather than vendoring it.
  6. Before the next descent: confirm nobody is carrying a piece in the Side Bag that their build needs live.

If co-op will not start

  • Both host and guest should finish the prologue and tutorial before trying to join.
  • Look for the village co-op access point after the tutorial rather than expecting an option on the title screen.
  • Confirm the invite actually reached your friend through Steam — the lobby uses Steam invites, not in-game lobby codes.

When the run feels worse than solo

SymptomReason recorded on this pageChange to make
Rooms take much longerEnemy pressure is reported to scale with the partyMatch the difficulty to the weakest member instead of adding players to a hard setting
One player keeps dying firstThat build has not come online yetGive that player the ranged or control row, which needs less uptime
Nobody is revivingRevive duty was never assignedName one reviver per down before the next floor
Tablets feel wastedLoot priorities were never agreedAgree who spends Tablets on what before the run, not after the drop
The session ends for everyoneProgress is host-authoritativeRecreate the lobby, as described on the multiplayer page
The four-player limit, item trading and revives are from the Steam listing; the monster-scaling behaviour is reported by a third-party review rather than stated officially, so treat it as a community observation.

Common mistakes

  • Adding players without changing the plan. Scaling raises pressure, and four damage builds still need a front line and a reviver.
  • Storing the core in the Side Bag. Stored items are inactive, Tablets included, so a full bag is not a finished build.
  • Splitting the revive. Two players on one prompt gives the enemy a free hit on both.
  • Trading for the future. Offer a piece to the teammate whose current core uses it now, not the one who might use it later.
  • Assuming shared credit. XP, currency and quest credit are not specified for co-op, so check your own save.

What this page does not cover

Lobby creation, invites and the host/guest split live on the multiplayer page. Artifact adjacency and the Side Bag rules are on Artifacts and Tablets, branch trade-offs on weapons, the difficulty gate on Hard Mode, and the costume trade-offs that decide who survives a first floor on costumes.

Quick FAQ

How many players can join?

Up to four, joined through Steam invites. The session belongs to the host, so the cap is a lobby limit rather than a difficulty setting.

Do enemies get harder with more players?

Reported to scale with the number of players. That observation comes from a third-party review rather than an official statement.

What is the biggest co-op advantage?

Revives. A death ends a solo run, while in co-op a teammate can bring you back mid-run, so a party that ignores that plays harder than solo.

Should the party trade everything?

No. Trade what you cannot use or what completes a teammate’s core, and keep the pieces your own board depends on.

Why did the run end when one player dropped?

Because progress is host-authoritative. If the host disconnects, the session goes with them, so the host’s connection is the party’s problem.
